metadata.title: Local Ranking Problem on the BrowseGraph

extraction_notes.note: The paper's findings are empirical observations read off tables and figures; the key ones are emitted as claim nodes with rigor numerical, while the tables and figures themselves (only in floats/images) are not nodes.

pseudocode_steps mis-parsed algorithm2e's two-body \eIf: it truncated the \For/\eIf step statements (ASP5, ASP7, ASP9) after the then-branch and parented the else-branch lines to ASP7. Overriding 'keep as returned', the three statements were re-sliced verbatim to their matching closing braces and the else-branch lines reparented to ASP9.
Dropped the comment-only pseudocode line (/* For each step ... */) and the trailing caption fragment after \Return as non-operations; steps renumbered.
LRP is stated both in the Introduction and in Related Work (Chen et al.); the Introduction's two-sentence formulation was kept as the single node.
theorem or remark: Bressan and Pretto's impossibility result is only summarized in words, but it is a cited result stated in full, so it is an external theorem.

sec:subgraphs.section: Subgraphs Based on Session Referrer URL

nodes.statement: We study the LRP problem on a BrowseGraph\ from a large news provider, considering as subgraphs the aggregations of browsing traces of users coming from different domains.
conclusions: We study the LRP problem on a BrowseGraph\ from a large news provider, considering as subgraphs the aggregations of browsing traces of users coming from different domains.

nodes.name: Same size referrer-based (SRB)
nodes.statement: item Same size referrer-based (SRB). To measure how much the different sizes of the graphs impact on the observed behavior, we fix a number of nodes and extract a portion of each subgraph in order to obtain exactly the same size for all networks. The selection is performed with several attempts of BFS expansion, starting from a random node in each graph, until the resulting graphs have very similar size (pm 9.4\%): other ways of selecting subgraphs would end up with disconnected samples, which of course would void the purpose of this experiment. With this procedure instead, we are able to compare the graphs on equal grounds and at the same time control for the effect of size (about 3K nodes and 20K edges).

nodes.name: Random (R)
nodes.statement: item Random (R). To check whether the observed behavior has to do with the user behavior underlying the graph under examination (e.g., the particular structure of the graph determined by the sessions of users coming from Twitter), we take a set of seven random graphs each of them reflecting the size of each of the referrer-based subgraphs. Thus, we can explore the behavior of browsing graphs, which preserve the size of the graphs originated by specific types of users, but that are ``artificial'' in the sense that destroy any connection with the behavior connected to a particular user class. To make sure that the size is the same, we start from a BFS exploration and we prune the last level to match exactly the size we need.
